summary_md: Paul's own unpublished client report (to Trey Hawkins and Hannah Benito; year not printed, 2026 inferred) surveys political money in financial services and makes three recommendations to Credit Unions: raise giving 41% over the 2023-2024 baseline to about $4.3M, push employee and middle-management giving to trade groups, and run campaigns that set CUs apart from banks. The extract only covers the Crypto and Community Banks sections. Crypto giving rose from $1.76M (2021-22) to $145.5M (2023-24). The text reports +8,162.6%, but the stated figures give about +8,167%. The C-suite share of that giving went from 69% to 98.8%, and super PACs took 71.9% of non-direct giving, which is itself 70% of the total. A 2025-26 projection of more than $175M would be a midterm-cycle rise, which the report attributes to the CLARITY Act. Crypto-backed candidates won 38 of 40 primaries, and opinion runs 31% oppose to 27% support (no source given). Community-bank member LDA activity rose by an average of 20 interactions. The method is descriptive throughout: no model, no uncertainty, no identification design. Against the system as built, the report matters in three places. (1) Mentat's cycle model applies a symmetric x1.8635 presidential factor to general giving on the midterm step. For a crypto-like industry that projects a large 2025-26 drop, the opposite of the report's projection. (2) The per-member LDA interaction counts look like the bill-roster join that the lobbying lane rejected as circular, and they use LDA as a weight source, which D-021 bars. (3) The super-PAC share and the C-suite share both point to gaps in what Mentat currently splits out. All new analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto industry giving projected north of $175M for 2025-2026 versus $145.5M in 2023-2024: an off-year (midterm) increase the report calls an outlier, attributed to the CLARITY Act push; normally spending is higher in presidential and lower in midterm cycles.
bearings.paper_location: Crypto section, line 9 of the text extract
bearings.system_side: General giving takes a fixed presidential factor u = 1.8635 on BOTH steps (D-121), so the 2025-26 midterm step is scaled by about 1/1.8635 (roughly -46%); company PACs keep fitted phi on the midterm step. A bill-driven regime shift like crypto's would be forecast in the wrong direction.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only if crypto (or any industry with a live legislative fight) is run through the general-giving measure; the report's $175M is itself a projection with no stated method, window or source, so it is a counterexample to check, not evidence.

bearings.paper_claim: 2026 LDA reports show members such as Zach Nunn, Andy Kim, Young Kim and Bill Huizenga with an average increase of 20 interactions within the year, read as the community-bank industry pushing harder.
bearings.system_side: LD-2 filings never name members; member attribution comes from crediting every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill, so P(joined given lobbied) = 1 by construction and the link is REFUTED as contact or influence evidence. The interaction ledger reproduces that join by design.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies if the report's interactions are bill-roster counts (the term matches lobby_interactions.py, whose docstring says it reuses that join; inferred, not stated in the report). If they came from description-named contacts, only the window and denominator flags remain.

bearings.paper_claim: Super PACs take 71.9% of crypto's non-direct-to-candidate giving, which is 70% of industry giving; Fairshake is called the 2nd largest super PAC and wholly crypto-funded; backed candidates won 38 of 40 primaries.
bearings.system_side: Mentat seeds the PAC transfer traversal from each industry's funded committees and partitions downstream beneficiary dollars into support/oppose/party; 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose and the attributed-estimate producer is unbuilt. The report counts super-PAC receipts as giving without that partition.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 38/40 win count has no window, no denominator of contested races and no baseline win rate; any reuse needs the support/oppose split by party and a stated cycle.

bearings.paper_claim: C-suite share of crypto donations rose from 69% (2021-22) to 98.8% (2023-24); the CU shortfall is framed as missing employee and middle-management giving.
bearings.system_side: Mentat assigns Schedule A rows to roster companies by employer key; occupation text enters only as an optional scoped regex on override rules, not as a role taxonomy, so no C-suite vs employee share is produced.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An occupation-role split would need a hand-coded precision check (Paul's literature cites SOC executive codes); the report gives no coding rule for C-suite.

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto outspends key allies by factors of 100, so CUs would have no chance in a monetary fight with the industry (supporting graph missing).
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head money term is saturating, (x+1)/((x+1)+HALFF*rcp), weighted by WM alongside a coalition term WP; a 100x dollar gap yields a bounded pull gap, and the dashboard reports 'cannot fully offset' only when q >= 1.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system's functional form is an assumption (share-type ratio) not validated against outcomes; the report's factor of 100 has no denominator or window, so neither side establishes the size of the disadvantage.

gaps_exposed: No industry-specific regime-shift term in the cycle model: a bill-driven midterm surge (crypto 2025-26) is forecast as a symmetric midterm drop under the general-giving factor.
Mentat produces no occupation-role (C-suite vs employee) split of individual giving, which the report's main CU recommendation depends on.
The support/oppose attributed-estimate producer for super-PAC money is unbuilt, so super-PAC share of industry giving cannot yet be read as support for candidates.
No primary-election outcome measure exists to test claims like 38 of 40 backed primaries won.
No independent member-level lobbying contact measure exists; per-member LDA counts can only come from the circular bill-roster join.
flags: D-021 and refuted lobbied-member link: per-member LDA interaction counts (average +20) use LDA as a member weight and, if from the bill-roster join, are circular by construction; do not cite as lobbying contact.

Window and denominator missing: factor of 100 outspending, average of 20 interactions (which members, which baseline year), 38 of 40 primaries (which cycles), 31% vs 27% opinion (no source), Fairshake rank 2 (no date or metric).
Arithmetic: $1.76M to $145.5M is about +8,167%, not the reported +8,162.6% (likely rounding of unrounded totals; unstated).
Causal and influence language without a design: CLARITY Act as the impetus, money buys attention, self-destructive feedback loop; all asserted, untested.
Coverage: abstract promises five industries but the extract contains only Crypto and Community Banks; the CU baseline dollar figure is not stated ($4.3M / 1.41 implies about $3.05M, derived).
Any agent recomputation here is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: No bibliography entries; this is Paul's own report. Its focus on employee giving and CU distinctiveness fits the built 16-PAC CU cohort. Two claims are stale against the system: the per-member LDA interaction counts rest on the bill-roster link the lobbying lane refuted as circular (and D-021 bars LDA as a weight), and the midterm crypto surge clashes with Mentat's symmetric general-giving midterm factor (D-121), which forecasts a decline. Money-buys-attention is untested here.

related.why: Same subject (crypto lobby and Fairshake-era spending); a published source the report's Crypto section could be checked against.
Furnas finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, while the report reads LDA activity and campaign giving as one advocacy push.
Experimental evidence on contributions and access is the nearest tested version of the report's money-buys-attention claim (access, not influence, per D-025 wording).
LobbyView bill-level LDA data underlies the bill-roster member join that the report's per-member interaction counts appear to rely on.
Documents election-cycle synchronization of lobbying, the cycle-phase assumption the report's off-year crypto surge departs from.
Tests the sequencing of donations and lobbying that the report assumes when combining FEC and LDA evidence.
